newsitem.title: USA: Managers are biggest obstacle to virtual offices.
newsitem.headline: Managers are biggest obstacle to virtual offices.

text.p: Workers tired of commuting who ask to work from home often are turned down by managers on grounds that it would be too difficult to appraise their productivity.

This type of reaction, according to John Frank, an expert on working from "virtual offices", is typical of many managers today. "Their attitude is, 'If I can't see you, you must not be working,' and their arrogance is going to cost them a person with top-notch skills," Frank said.
"Most likely, the only thing that is preventing that computer expert from doing his job from home is that his manager doesn't have a clue how virtual office technology can be utilized," Frank said.

These managers may soon be left behind. A new study by consultants KMPG Peat Marwick of 106 human resource executives at the largest U.S. companies found that nearly one in four have employees who regularly telecommute either part- or full-time.

What is more, 53 percent of the firms with telecommuters said workers enjoyed "increased productivity and job satisfaction" and one-third reported "lower real estate costs and reduced employee turnover."

KPMG's Joseph Parente, who heads its telecommuting practice, said the trend "began with entrepreneurial companies and new technology companies and now it is becoming more common in corporate America."
Capitalising on this development is Frank's Schaumburg, Illinois-based Actoras Consulting Group (ACG), which guides firms into the virtual office age.
Frank defines virtual office as technology "enabling workers to work anywhere, anytime." The arrangement commonly requires a laptop computer and a modem to communicate with a company's office.
While many virtual offices are located in the employee's home, they can also be at a customer site, in an airport or in leased office space that is part of a shared business centre.

"There are a lot of different views as to what it means to work virtually," Frank said, noting that estimates of the number of Americans who work in virtual offices range from 3 million to 12 million.
"In my mind it has less to do with the technology and more to do with the sorts of operational processes companies employ to allow their workers to work more efficiently," he said.
Prior to founding his consulting firm a year ago, Frank led IBM's campaign to relocate employees to virtual offices.

About 20,000 of the 118,000 U.S. employees at International Business Machines Corp. now work at home, from customer locations or in satellite offices. The change, which boosted productivity 10 percent on average, was initiated as a cost-cutting step, but turned out to be a money-maker for IBM.
Managers who ask how they would track the productivity of a virtual office worker are admitting they do not know what their employees are doing today, Frank said.

"If they had an objective performance appraisal system it wouldn't matter if the employee was working in the office or halfway across the country. Are we managing people by what we see them doing or by what output they're generating?"
Frank said managers need to be rewarded based on the productivity of those who report to them.
"We've got a shortage of skilled workers coming up," Frank said. Many of those workers are going to say 'I work for you out of my home or I don't work for you anymore'," he said.
By the year 2010, Frank estimated, as many as 30 percent of the nation's work force "will work out of virtual offices."

That is because virtual offices do more than reduce corporate space costs and improve productivity, Frank said. He credits them for cutting commuting time and air pollution and even saving employees money on clothing and lunches.
"If I owned a big company today I would not be building a big office building," Frank said.
(Sherwood Ross is a free-lance writer who covers workplace topics for Reuters. Any opinions in this column are his alone).
